T0B06.explanation: The minimum safe distance from a power line when installing an antenna is enough so that if the antenna falls, no part of it can come closer than 10 feet to the power wires. This safety margin accounts for the worst-case scenario of the antenna or its support structure falling. Contact with power lines can be fatal.

T0B07.hint: Never climb a crank-up tower unless it is fully retracted or has mechanical locks engaged.
T0B07.explanation: An important safety rule for crank-up towers is that they must not be climbed unless retracted or with mechanical safety locking devices installed. Crank-up towers can collapse if the lifting mechanism fails while someone is on an extended tower. Always retract the tower or engage positive mechanical locks before climbing.

T0B08.hint: Each tower leg gets its own ground rod, and all rods are bonded together.
T0B08.explanation: A proper grounding method for a tower is separate eight-foot ground rods for each tower leg, bonded to the tower and each other. This provides a low-impedance path to earth for lightning energy. A single short ground rod is insufficient, and all ground points must be bonded together to equalize voltage during a strike.

T0B09.hint: Utility poles carry high-voltage power lines -- putting an antenna on one is extremely dangerous.
T0B09.explanation: You should avoid attaching an antenna to a utility pole because the antenna could contact high-voltage power lines. Utility poles carry dangerous voltages, and working near them or attaching antennas to them creates a serious risk of electrocution. Always install antennas on structures well away from power lines.

T0B10.hint: Sharp bends in lightning ground wires act as inductors and impede the flow of high-frequency lightning energy.
T0B10.explanation: When installing grounding conductors for lightning protection, sharp bends must be avoided. Sharp bends increase the impedance of the conductor at the high frequencies present in lightning strikes. Lightning current tends to jump across sharp bends rather than follow them, reducing the effectiveness of the ground system.

T0B11.hint: Your local building codes govern how towers and antennas must be grounded.
T0B11.explanation: Local electrical codes establish grounding requirements for amateur radio towers and antennas. While the FCC regulates radio operations, the physical installation of towers and their electrical grounding falls under local building and electrical codes. These codes ensure safe installation practices appropriate for local conditions.

T0C01.hint: Radio waves are electromagnetic radiation but do not have enough energy to ionize atoms.
T0C01.explanation: Radio signals are non-ionizing radiation. Unlike gamma rays, X-rays, and alpha particles, radio waves do not have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms or break chemical bonds. While RF energy can cause heating effects at high power levels, it does not cause the cellular damage associated with ionizing radiation.

T0C02.hint: The human body absorbs RF energy most efficiently around 50 MHz, making exposure limits strictest there.
T0C02.explanation: Maximum permissible exposure has the lowest value (most restrictive limit) at 50 MHz. The human body resonates and absorbs RF energy most efficiently in the 30-300 MHz range, with peak absorption near 50 MHz for a standing adult. Because more energy is absorbed, exposure limits must be lower at these frequencies.

T0C03.hint: If you transmit only half the time, the average exposure is halved, so the limit doubles.
T0C03.explanation: If duty cycle changes from 100% to 50%, the allowable power density increases by a factor of 2. Since exposure limits are based on average exposure over time, transmitting only 50% of the time means the average RF exposure is half of what it would be at 100% duty cycle. Therefore, twice the instantaneous power density is allowed.

T0C04.hint: Frequency, power, distance, and antenna pattern all play a role in how much RF energy a person is exposed to.
T0C04.explanation: All the listed factors affect RF exposure: frequency and power level of the RF field, distance from the antenna, and radiation pattern of the antenna. Higher power, closer distance, and being in the main beam of the antenna all increase exposure. RF safety analysis must consider all these factors together.

T0C05.hint: Your body absorbs different amounts of RF energy at different frequencies.
T0C05.explanation: Exposure limits vary with frequency because the human body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than at others. The body acts as an antenna, and its absorption characteristics change with frequency. Peak absorption occurs when body dimensions are resonant with the wavelength, typically around 30-100 MHz.

T0C06.hint: You can verify compliance through calculation, computer modeling, or actual measurement.
T0C06.explanation: All the listed methods are acceptable for determining compliance with FCC RF exposure regulations: calculation based on FCC OET Bulletin 65, calculation based on computer modeling, and measurement of field strength using calibrated equipment. Any of these approaches can be used to demonstrate that exposure levels are within safe limits.

T0C07.hint: Concentrated RF energy at the antenna can burn your skin on contact.
T0C07.explanation: Touching an antenna during transmission creates a hazard of RF burn to the skin. The high concentration of RF energy at the antenna can cause localized heating of tissue at the point of contact, resulting in painful burns. Always ensure no one can touch the antenna while transmitting.

T0C08.hint: Moving the antenna farther from people is the most effective way to reduce exposure.
T0C08.explanation: Relocating antennas can reduce exposure to RF radiation. Since RF field strength decreases rapidly with distance (inverse square law), moving antennas higher or farther from occupied areas is one of the most effective ways to reduce exposure. Relocating the transmitter or increasing duty cycle would not help.

T0C09.hint: Any time you change your antenna or transmitter setup, you need to recheck your RF safety compliance.
T0C09.explanation: To keep your station in compliance with RF safety regulations, re-evaluate the station whenever an item in the transmitter or antenna system is changed. Changes in power level, antenna type, antenna height, or feed line can all affect RF exposure levels. A new evaluation ensures continued compliance after any modification.

T0C10.hint: Duty cycle matters because it determines how much RF energy a person is exposed to on average.
T0C10.explanation: Duty cycle is used to determine safe RF exposure levels because it affects the average exposure to radiation. Since RF safety limits are based on average exposure over time, a lower duty cycle (less time transmitting) means lower average exposure. CW and SSB modes have lower duty cycles than FM, for example.

T0C11.hint: Duty cycle is simply what fraction of time the transmitter is actually transmitting.
T0C11.explanation: Duty cycle during the averaging time for RF exposure is defined as the percentage of time that a transmitter is transmitting. If you transmit for 3 minutes out of every 6 minutes, your duty cycle is 50%. Lower duty cycles mean lower average RF exposure, which is favorable for RF safety compliance.

T0C12.hint: RF radiation lacks the energy to damage DNA or cause chemical changes in cells.
T0C12.explanation: RF radiation differs from ionizing radiation (radioactivity) because RF radiation does not have sufficient energy to cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA. Ionizing radiation (like gamma rays and X-rays) has enough energy to break molecular bonds, but RF energy can only cause heating effects. This is a fundamental difference in their biological impact.

T0C13.hint: The person who holds the license bears the responsibility for RF safety at their station.
T0C13.explanation: The station licensee is responsible for ensuring that no person is exposed to RF energy above the FCC exposure limits. This obligation requires the licensee to evaluate their station's RF exposure levels and take steps to ensure compliance. It is not the FCC's, the public's, or any local authority's responsibility -- it falls squarely on the licensee.
